cards.titel: AVM vs. aneurysm: epidemiology and presentation
cards.notiz: Greenberg p. 1505. Most common genetic cause of AVMs: HHT (15–20% of HHT patients have cerebral AVMs). Seizures ≈ 34%.

cards.titel: AVM annual hemorrhage rate by risk factors (Stapf)
cards.notiz: Greenberg p. 1506. Strongest predictor = **previous rupture** (1.3%/y unruptured vs. 4.3%/y ruptured). Exclusively deep drainage 1.6–2.4×; risk ↑ 30% per decade of age. Unselected annual risk ≈ 2.3%/y.

cards.text: Lifetime AVM hemorrhage risk: exact formula = 1 − ({{c1::annual risk of not bleeding}})^{{c2::remaining years of life}}; simple approximation (3%/y): risk (%) ≈ {{c3::105 − age in years}}.

cards.notiz: Greenberg p. 1510. L-Y score 1–5, added to S-M grade; predicts postoperative mRS change better than S-M alone. S-M III with low L-Y behaves like S-M II, with high L-Y like S-M IV.

cards.rueckseite:
- **Class A (S-M I–II):** surgical resection
- **Class B (S-M III):** multimodality treatment (use Lawton–Young to refine)
- **Class C (S-M IV–V):** observe, repeat angiogram every 5 years; treat only for progressive deficit, steal symptoms or aneurysms found on surveillance

**A Randomized trial of Unruptured Brain AVMs:** medical management alone vs. medical management + intervention (surgery, SRS, embolization or combination). Stopped early: **medical management alone superior** (fewer stroke/death events).
Heavily criticized: short follow-up, premature closure, few surgical cases, heterogeneous intervention; conclusion not uniformly accepted.

cards.vorderseite: Stereotactic radiosurgery for AVM: key facts
cards.rueckseite:
- Indication: small (nidus **≤ 2.5–3 cm**), deep or eloquent AVMs
- **Obliteration 70–80% over 1–3 years**
- **Latency period:** bleeding risk ≈ natural history (1–3%/y) until obliteration
- Delayed effects: radiation necrosis, edema, cyst formation; permanent deficits 2–3%
- **Embolization before SRS lowers obliteration** (≈ 70% → 47%)
- Follow-up: MRI/MRA every 6 months; confirm obliteration with catheter angiography
cards.notiz: Greenberg p. 1510–1512. Conventional fractionated radiation is effective in ≤ 20% only.

cards.rueckseite:
1. Wide exposure
2. **Occlude feeding arteries before draining veins** (premature venous occlusion → swelling/rupture)
3. **Remove the entire nidus** (feeder ligation alone does not protect)
4. Spare en passant vessels
5. Dissect directly on the nidus, use sulci and fissures
6. High-flow lesions: consider preoperative embolization (24–48 h before)
7. Multiple territories: consider staging
8. Clip accessible feeding-artery aneurysms
Confirm complete removal with intra-/early postoperative angiography.

- **Normal perfusion pressure breakthrough:** post-op swelling/hemorrhage from loss of autoregulation in chronically hypoperfused brain; prevention: **propranolol 20 mg PO QID for 3 days pre-op**, labetalol to keep MAP 70–80 mmHg
- **Occlusive hyperemia:** obstruction of venous outflow of adjacent brain (or delayed thrombosis of draining vein/sinus); worse if patient kept "dry"
- Rebleeding from **retained nidus**
- Seizures

Tuft of medullary veins converging into an enlarged collector vein (**caput medusae**), with **normal brain between the vessels**; low-flow, low-pressure, no arterial component. Drains normal brain.
Rarely symptomatic; if symptoms → look for an associated **cavernous malformation** (SWI/GRE).
**Do not resect** (risk of venous infarction); when operating on an adjacent cavernoma, preserve the DVA.

cards.vorderseite: Dural AV fistula: epidemiology, etiology and locations
cards.rueckseite:
- 10–15% of intracranial AV shunts; 61–66% women, usually 40s–50s
- **Acquired:** strongly associated with **venous sinus thrombosis** (sinus occlusion opens dormant dural channels / venous hypertension drives angiogenesis)
- Most common site: **transverse–sigmoid junction** (63%), then tentorial/petrosal, anterior fossa/ethmoidal, middle fossa, cavernous sinus, SSS, foramen magnum
- Most common symptom: **pulsatile tinnitus** (+ occipital bruit)
- Diagnosis: full **6-vessel angiography** (both ICA, ECA, VA)

cards.vorderseite: DAVF: natural history and indications for treatment
cards.rueckseite:
Cortical venous drainage (CVD) separates benign from aggressive fistulas.
- **Without CVD:** 98% remain benign (≈ 2% develop CVD) → follow; restudy if bruit changes
- **With CVD:** annual hemorrhage **8.1%**, nonhemorrhagic deficit 6.9%, mortality 10.4%
- Most aggressive location: **tentorial**, then middle fossa and anterior fossa/ethmoidal
Indications: CVD, neurologic deficit, hemorrhage, orbital venous congestion, refractory tinnitus/headache. Locations favoring **surgery: ethmoidal and tentorial**.

Congenital AV fistula into the **median prosencephalic vein** (embryonic precursor), fed by choroidal, mesencephalic, pericallosal arteries; often absent straight sinus.
- **Neonate:** high-output **heart failure**, cranial bruit
- **Infant:** macrocephaly/**hydrocephalus** (aqueduct compression or venous hypertension), prominent scalp veins
- Untreated: ≈ 100% neonatal mortality
- Treatment: staged **endovascular embolization**; shunt if hydrocephalus
Parenchymal AVMs draining into the VOG show retrograde filling of the internal cerebral vein.

Found in 1.2% of asymptomatic people but in up to **23% of patients with pulsatile tinnitus** (ipsilateral); more common in women.
Treatment if masking fails: **transmastoid resurfacing** (reconstruct sinus wall with bone, fascia, glue), endovascular coiling/stenting, or clip reconstruction.

cards.notiz: Greenberg p. 1526. Autosomal dominant; familial cases often have multiple lesions and form new ones (0.4–2.7 new CMs/year).
Greenberg p. 1528. Types I, II, V = high risk; III intermediate; IV lowest. Rates from pediatric series (Nikoubashman).
Greenberg p. 1536. The gap between loss of function and cell death defines the **penumbra**.

cards.vorderseite: Cerebrovascular reserve: acetazolamide challenge and misery perfusion
cards.rueckseite:
Response of CBF to **1 g IV acetazolamide**:
- **Type I:** normal baseline, ↑ 30–60%
- **Type II:** reduced baseline, blunted ↑ (< 10%)
- **Type III:** reduced baseline, **paradoxical ↓** (steal; vessels already maximally dilated)
**Misery perfusion:** autoregulation exhausted → **↑ oxygen extraction fraction (OEF on PET)**; independent predictor of stroke (St. Louis Carotid Occlusion Study: 26% vs. 5% 2-year ipsilateral stroke).

1. **Circle of Willis:** contralateral ICA via ACom; posterior circulation via PComm
2. **Retrograde ophthalmic artery** from ECA: facial → angular a.; maxillary → middle meningeal → lacrimal a.; STA → supraorbital a.
3. Maxillary → anterior tympanic → caroticotympanic branch of ICA
4. Cortical–cortical (leptomeningeal) anastomoses
5. Dural–leptomeningeal anastomoses
Vertebral occlusion: occipital a. → muscular VA branches; ascending cervical a.

Basis pontis or genu of internal capsule
cards.notiz: Greenberg p. 1540–1541. Lacunes 3–20 mm from lipohyalinosis of penetrators (hypertension). Aphasia, hemianopsia, seizures or coma virtually exclude a lacune.

cards.vorderseite: Ischemic stroke in young adults: causes
cards.rueckseite:
Only 3% of ischemic strokes < 40 y. **Trauma** is the most common cause < 45 y. Otherwise:
- Atherosclerosis 20% (diabetics, smokers)
- **Cardioembolism 20%** (valve disease, endocarditis, a-fib, myxoma, **PFO paradoxical embolism**)
- Vasculopathy 10% (**dissection**, FMD, moyamoya, vasculitis, drugs)
- Coagulopathy 10% (**antiphospholipid syndrome**, protein C/S deficiency, sickle cell)
- Peripartum 5%
- Other 35%: oral contraceptives, CVT, migraine, cocaine, PRES
cards.notiz: Greenberg p. 1541–1543. Antiphospholipid syndrome: warfarin INR ≥ 3; aspirin ineffective.

cards.rueckseite:
- **Cranial nerve injury** (most common, up to 8–10%): **XII** (tongue deviates to injured side; bilateral → airway obstruction), vagus/RLN (vocal cord), marginal mandibular branch of VII
- **Stroke** ≈ 5%: minor deficits mostly embolic; major stroke mostly **post-op ICA occlusion**
- **Hyperperfusion syndrome:** ipsilateral headache/eye pain, seizures, ICH days after surgery (severe stenosis, poor collaterals) → strict BP control
- Neck hematoma (asphyxiation risk), late false aneurysm
- Hoarseness (usually laryngeal edema), BP lability (baroreceptor loss), restenosis (fibrous hyperplasia < 2 y)
cards.notiz: Greenberg p. 1567–1568. Unilateral XII palsy → postpone contralateral CEA until recovery.

cards.vorderseite: Totally occluded ICA and carotid stump syndrome
cards.rueckseite:
Found in 10–15% of carotid-territory TIA/stroke. Symptomatic occlusion: **≈ 7%/y stroke** (5.9% ipsilateral) despite antithrombotics; asymptomatic occlusion: negligible risk.
Stroke patterns: whole hemisphere, **watershed infarct**, carotid stump syndrome.
**Stump syndrome:** ongoing ipsilateral symptoms from emboli from the stump reaching the MCA via ECA–ICA collaterals → stump excision or stenting (± ECA endarterectomy).
Chronic occlusions: poor patency after reopening.

12% have a second embolism within 2 weeks, but early anticoagulation risks **hemorrhagic transformation** (mostly within 48 h).
- Do **not** start within the first **48 h**
- Repeat **CT after 48 h** before starting
- **No anticoagulation for large infarcts**
A-fib: 4.5%/y stroke untreated; risk stratified by CHADS₂ (anticoagulate if ≥ 2).

**5 D's:** drop attacks, diplopia, dysarthria, defect (homonymous visual field), dizziness.
Clinical diagnosis needs ≥ 2 of: bilateral motor/sensory symptoms in one event, diplopia, dysarthria, homonymous hemianopsia.
Causes: hemodynamic (subclavian steal, bilateral VA stenosis or one hypoplastic VA), embolism, perforator occlusion; atheroma mostly at the **VA origin**.
Stroke risk 4.5–7%/y. Surgery: VA endarterectomy, **VA-to-CCA transposition**, OA–PICA bypass.

Positional VBI from **VA occlusion with head rotation**, usually the VA **contralateral** to the direction of rotation, at **C1–2**; symptomatic mostly when the occluded VA is dominant and PComms are incompetent.
Diagnosis: **dynamic catheter angiography** with head turning.
Treatment: anticoagulation/collar → **VA decompression** (C1 hemilaminectomy, keeps motion, ≈ 33% persistent symptoms) first; if it fails → **C1–2 fusion** (high success, loses 50–70% of rotation).

- **Anticoagulation** with UFH or LMWH, even with **hemorrhagic infarct/ICH**, then VKA (INR 2–3); pregnancy: LMWH
- **Endovascular** thrombolysis/thrombectomy: deterioration despite anticoagulation, coma, deep CVT, contraindication to anticoagulation
- **Decompressive craniectomy** for herniation from mass effect
- ICP: **acetazolamide**, CSF drainage; osmotic diuretics last (↑ viscosity)
- Seizure: treat (no prophylaxis); **no steroids**
- Protect vision (serial LP, ONSF, shunt)
cards.notiz: Greenberg p. 1599–1600. ≈ 13% die or remain dependent despite anticoagulation; poor prognosis: coma, deep venous involvement, hemorrhage, extremes of age.

zeilen: LMWH throughout + ≥ 6 weeks postpartum (≥ 6 months total)
cards.notiz: Greenberg p. 1600. Future pregnancy not contraindicated; LMWH prophylaxis in later pregnancies.

cards.rueckseite:
- **EC/IC Bypass Study (1985):** STA–MCA vs. aspirin; 96% patency but **no benefit** (did not select hemodynamic failure)
- **COSS:** symptomatic ICA occlusion + ↑ OEF; stopped for futility (14.4% 30-day event rate)
- **JET:** fewer strokes after bypass in hemodynamically selected patients
Indications today: hemodynamic insufficiency (misery perfusion), **complex aneurysms needing parent vessel sacrifice**, tumors encasing arteries, **moyamoya**.

cards.notiz: Greenberg p. 1602. Need for bypass assessed by balloon test occlusion with hypotensive challenge.

Greenberg p. 1609. Putaminal ICH: lenticulostriates (Charcot–Bouchard microaneurysms). IVH in ≈ 45% of sICH, independent predictor of poor outcome. Lobar ICH: think CAA (elderly), AVM, tumor, hemorrhagic infarct.

cards.text: ICH hematoma expansion: {{c1::33–38%}} within 1–3 h of onset, falling to ≈ 16% at 3–6 h. The CTA {{c2::"spot sign"}} (small enhancing focus inside the clot) predicts expansion. Guideline BP target for SBP 150–200: lower to {{c3::140 mmHg}}; INTERACT-2/ATACH-2 showed more {{c4::renal adverse events}} with SBP < 140.

cards.rueckseite:
- **Warfarin-associated lobar ICH** with nonvalvular a-fib: avoid long-term anticoagulation (high recurrence, CAA)
- Strong indication: consider anticoagulation after **nonlobar** ICH
- Avoid oral anticoagulants for **≥ 4 weeks** after OAC-associated ICH (no mechanical valve)
- **Aspirin monotherapy** can be resumed within days
- DVT prophylaxis: pneumatic compression from day 1; low-dose heparin after 1–4 days once bleeding has stopped

cards.vorderseite: Supratentorial ICH: factors for and against surgery
cards.rueckseite:
**Favor surgery:** marked mass effect/shift, symptoms from mass effect or ICP, volume **≈ 10–30 mL**, rapid deterioration, superficial **lobar** location, non-dominant side, **young patient**, early (< 24 h).
**Against:** small clot (< 10 mL), minimal symptoms, **GCS ≤ 5**/loss of brainstem reflexes, huge clot (> 60 mL with GCS ≤ 8 → 91% 30-day mortality; > 85 mL → no survivors), age > 75, deep **putaminal/thalamic** ICH, severe coagulopathy.

- **≤ 3 cm**, no compression: conservative
- **> 3 cm** with **hydrocephalus or brainstem compression** → surgical evacuation ASAP
- **EVD alone without evacuation is not recommended** (risk of upward herniation)
- Absent brainstem reflexes + flaccid quadriplegia: intensive therapy usually not indicated

cards.titel: Spontaneous ICH in young adults (15–45 y): causes
cards.notiz: Greenberg p. 1630. Lobar ICH in a young patient → suspect AVM (37.5% of lobar bleeds). Also consider eclampsia, CVT, leukemia, HSV encephalitis.
